newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico bankers fear left's economic plan - papers.
newsitem.headline: Mexico bankers fear left's economic plan - papers.

text.p: Mexico's banking association chief said the private sector fears the economic program of the Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), a left-wing party seen as gaining ground nationally and leading the race for Mexico City mayor.

Antonio del Valle, the Mexican Banking Association chairman, was reported in several dailies as saying if the left-wing party's economic program was put into effect it would cause crises worse than in 1995, triggering a massive capital flight and runaway inflation.

Although the party is unlikely to gain control of Congress in key mid-term elections July 6 and the next presidential elections are not until 2000, the PRD's surge in popularity has caused an increased focus on the details of its programs, especially economic plans.
Valle said he spotlighted the PRD economic program since he believed the electorate should make a reasoned choice in next month's vote.
"What worries the private sector most, not only the country's bankers, is the (PRD's) economic program," Del Valle was reported as saying.
Del Valle said one of the economic proposals of the PRD is to "reduce" foreign debt payments by a little more than half the amounts currently paid.

"The only Mexican president that proposed non-payment of foreign debts was (Jose) Lopez Portillo in 1982. That year there was a devaluation of 600 percent, inflation more than 100 percent and a really massive flight of capital," he said.

Del Valle challenged PRD economists to debate. "We are open to debate with the economists of the PRD. And, yes, it would interest us if it were before the elections, so that the electorate had elements to judge and make a reasoned choice..." he added.
Valle recognised that the PRD leader Cuauhtemoc Cardenas had a "great opportunity" of winning the mayorship of Mexico City in the vote.
But added there were few chances of the party gaining majority control of Congress in the vote next month.

On July 6, voters will elect the whole of congress, a third of the Senate, six state governors and the mayor of Mexico City. It will be the first time ever residents of the capital will elect the post, which previously has been hand picked by the president.
